extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and practitioners interested in sketch comedy (performers, writers, historians)
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of the sketch-comedy genre: its form, typical length, performance modes, media/venues, historical origins, and common structural choices such as recurring characters or unrelated vignettes. Useful for people creating, performing, or studying sketch comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition / basic form
rubrics_metrics.description: "Sketch comedy comprises a series of short, amusing scenes or vignettes, called 'sketches' or 'skits'..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page frames sketch comedy as made up of distinct short scenes or vignettes rather than a continuous narrative; this is the fundamental structural expectation for the genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical duration
rubrics_metrics.description: "commonly between one and ten minutes long"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketches are generally brief; producers, writers and performers typically aim for sketches in this short range to fit variety shows, TV formats, live revues, and festival slots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance ensemble
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketches are "performed by a group of comic actors or comedians."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch comedy is usually troupe-based rather than a single stand-up performer; ensemble casting, character interplay and quick role changes are common production expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of creation and delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: "The sketches may be improvised live by the performers, developed through improvisation before public performance, or scripted and rehearsed in advance like a play."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable approaches include fully improvised work, improv-developed scripted sketches, and fully scripted/rehearsed sketches; the page highlights all three as valid methods of creation/delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical media/venues
rubrics_metrics.description: "...used widely in variety shows, as well as in late night talk shows and some sitcoms..." and also appears on stage, radio, television, film and animation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketches should be adaptable to multiple venues — live revues, radio segments, television sketch shows, late-night monologues, animated sketches and sketch films; format/length/content expectations shift with medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience and content target
rubrics_metrics.description: "While sketch comedy is now associated mostly with adult entertainment, certain children's television series have also used it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketches frequently target adult audiences but can be adapted for children; creators should choose tone, language and references appropriate to intended audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standalone vs themed/recurring structure
rubrics_metrics.description: "While separate sketches historically have tended to be unrelated, more recent groups have introduced overarching themes that connect the sketches within a particular show with recurring characters that return for more than one appearance."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both formats are valid: unrelated, one-off sketches or shows built around recurring characters/themes. Recurring characters can provide cohesion across episodes and allow character development and callbacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring characters and spinoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples such as Mr. Gumby, Ted and Ralph, The Family, and Saturday Night Live's recurring characters demonstrate that recurring characters "have notably been featured in a number of spinoff films, including The Blues Brothers (1980), Wayne's World (1992) and Superstar (1999)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recurring characters can become intellectual-property anchors for wider commercial opportunities (merchandise, films, spinoffs); creators may design sketches with potential recurring-character longevity in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvisational lineage and training influence
rubrics_metrics.description: "In North America, contemporary sketch comedy is largely an outgrowth of the improvisational comedy scene that flourished during the 1970s..." (The Second City, Upright Citizens Brigade, The Groundlings, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many modern sketch troupes stem from improv schools/companies; improvisational techniques and training strongly influence writing, rehearsal and performance practices in sketch comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sketch films and adaptations
rubrics_metrics.description: The page lists sketch films and film adaptations (e.g., Monty Python's And Now for Something Completely Different, The Meaning of Life; The Kentucky Fried Movie; more recent films like Movie 43).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch material can be compiled or adapted into feature-length films or anthology movies; structuring content for cinematic compilation or linking sketches for film requires different pacing and transitions than live/TV sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Festival and revue presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Many sketch revues included seasons at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival; noted festivals include Chicago Sketch Fest, SF Sketchfest, Toronto Sketch Comedy Festival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Festivals and fringe revues are important venues for sketch comedy exposure; creators may tailor sketches for festival constraints (time slots, audience mix, touring).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of subgenres and comedic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: The article's taxonomy and 'Subgenres' section situates sketch comedy within many subgenres and devices (e.g., alternative, character, slapstick, surreal, deadpan, parody, visual gag, wordplay, satire, impersonation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketches commonly draw on a wide range of comedic modes — creators choose devices (physical gag, satire, wordplay, character-based humor, etc.) to suit tone, audience and medium.
